title: Act V, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: Defeated, Brutus asks Clitus, Dardanius and Volumnius in turn to help him die; all refuse. He tells them Caesar's ghost appeared to him again at Philippi. Strato holds his sword and Brutus runs on it, saying 'Caesar, now be still: I kill'd not thee with half so good a will.' Antony and Octavius arrive. Antony calls Brutus 'the noblest Roman of them all,' the only conspirator who acted for the common good, not envy. Octavius orders an honorable burial and ends the play.

context.history: Plutarch reports that Brutus died by his own hand after Philippi, assisted by Strato, in 42 BC. Octavius later became Augustus, Rome's first emperor, ending the republic Brutus tried to save.

significance: The play closes with Antony's tribute, which reframes Brutus. Irony: the act meant to preserve the republic helped bring about the empire. Note: this scene depicts suicide; use safe messaging and offer support.
